body.heading: Walking, with somewhere for the mind to be
paragraphs: Many people find sitting meditation hard and walking easy, yet their walks get colonised by the same rumination they were escaping: the mind rehearses arguments while the feet go unnoticed around the block. A noticing walk gives the mind a light job, so the walk can do its work.
The job is simply to notice, in a chosen category, as you go. Not to photograph, not to achieve — just to let your attention graze on the world instead of the worry.

body.heading: Choose a lens for the walk
paragraphs: Pick one lens before you set off. Colours: find every shade of green, or hunt for things that are red. Sounds: count how many different ones you can hear, near and far. Shapes: round things, straight lines, things that are moving slowly. Or new things: details on your own street you have genuinely never seen, which is a more humbling game than it sounds.
When your mind wanders off to its rehearsals — it will — the lens is your way back. Oh yes: I was looking for round things. No scolding required; the lens just quietly re-offers itself.

body.heading: Short counts as much as long
paragraphs: Ten minutes around the block with a lens is a complete practice. So is the walk from the station done in noticing mode. The length matters far less than the quality of the attention, and a daily ten will teach you more than a monthly hour.

Over weeks, something subtle changes: the noticing starts leaking into the rest of the day. You catch the colour of a stranger’s coat, the exact sound of rain starting. The world was always this detailed. The walk just trained you to receive it.

takeaway: Give the walk a lens — a colour, a sound, a shape — and let the street do the rest.
